169.title: The bee (49–52)
169.hook: as the bee takes nectar and leaves the flower unharmed; look to your own faults, not others'
169.tomorrow: The lotus on the rubbish heap (53–59)
169.howItsDone: Theravada monks still go on alms rounds, receiving small amounts of food from many households, and teachers cite the bee verse as a picture of taking from the world without harm.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the garland-maker, and your line: pick the flower. Which teaching did you pick up and use? Day one hundred sixty-nine.
screen: `THE GARLAND-MAKER — PICK THE FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Watch a bee in a garden for one minute. It lands on a flower, pushes in, takes what it came for, and lifts off. Then look at the flower. It's still there. Same petals, same color, same scent, still open for the next bee. If anything, it's better off: the bee carried its pollen along. A lot of taking doesn't work that way. We take, and something is used up, bruised, left worse. The Dhammapada watched the same garden and found a whole way of living in it. Today, verses forty-nine to fifty-two: the bee.
screen: `ONE MINUTE WITH A BEE.` → `THE FLOWER IS STILL THERE.` → `A WHOLE WAY OF LIVING.`

segments.voice: Verse forty-nine, in Müller's English: “As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village.” The first picture is a monk on his alms round. He walks into the village, receives a little food from each house, and leaves without being a burden to anyone. Taking only what's offered, leaving every household as whole as he found it. But the verse reaches anyone who depends on others, which is everyone. Can you take what you need, from your family, your coworkers, the earth, and leave them unharmed? Verse fifty turns the bee's attention inward. Don't look at the faults of others, it says, what they've done and left undone. Look at what you yourself have done and left undone. The bee doesn't inspect the flower for flaws. It takes the nectar and goes. Then verses fifty-one and fifty-two, a twin pair about words. Verse fifty-one: “Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly.” Verse fifty-two is the flower with color and scent: good words from someone who lives them. You've met that idea before, in the cowherd. The flower chapter gives it a new picture. Words without practice are a lovely bloom that smells of nothing. So the bee teaches three things. Take without harming. Mind your own faults, not the flower's. And let your words carry some scent: something lived behind them.
screen: `TAKE, AND LEAVE THE FLOWER WHOLE.` · `THE MONK ON HIS ALMS ROUND.` · `YOUR OWN FAULTS, NOT OTHERS'.` · `A FLOWER WITHOUT SCENT.` · then, large: `THE BEE LEAVES THE FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle into the breath. Think of the places you'll take something from today. Food from the kitchen. Time and help from a coworker. Patience from someone at home. Water, power, a seat on the bus. For each, imagine being the bee: taking what you need, and leaving it whole. What would that look like? A thank-you. Cleaning up after yourself. Not taking the last of something. Choose one place, and hold that picture while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
The bee. Taking the nectar and leaving the flower unharmed: living among others without using them up.
screen: `THE BEE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the bee leaves the flower. Today, take what you need somewhere, and leave it as whole as you found it, or better. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

170.title: The lotus on the rubbish heap (53–59)
170.word: The lotus on the rubbish heap
170.hook: the scent of virtue travels against the wind; a lotus grows on a heap by the road
170.howItsDone: The lotus rising from mud is a Buddhist symbol seen in temple art and offerings, and teachers use the rubbish-heap verses to say that awakening can grow from ordinary, difficult life.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bee, and your line: the bee leaves the flower. Where did you take something and leave it whole? Day one hundred seventy, the last day of the flower chapter.
screen: `THE BEE — THE BEE LEAVES THE FLOWER.`

segments.voice: A bakery on a cold morning sends the smell of bread half a block down the street. But only downwind. Walk upwind of the bakery and there's nothing. Scent goes where the wind goes. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, once asked him a question about exactly this. Is there any scent, anywhere, that can travel against the wind? The answer closes the flower chapter. Today, verses fifty-three to fifty-nine: the lotus on the rubbish heap.
screen: `BREAD, HALF A BLOCK AWAY.` → `ONLY IF YOU'RE DOWNWIND.` → `ANY SCENT AGAINST THE WIND?`

segments.voice: Verse fifty-four gives the answer. The scent of flowers doesn't travel against the wind, not even sandalwood or jasmine, “but the odour of good people travels even against the wind.” Goodness is the one fragrance that goes everywhere. People hear about a kind person in places the person has never been. Verse fifty-three sets it up: as many garlands can be made from a heap of flowers, so much good can be done by someone once they're born. Verses fifty-five to fifty-seven add that among all perfumes, sandal, lotus and the rest, the scent of virtue is the highest, and that Mara can't even find the path of those who live well. Then the chapter ends on a picture of its own. Verses fifty-eight and fifty-nine: “as on a heap of rubbish cast upon the highway the lily will grow full of sweet perfume and delight.” Müller wrote lily. The Pali says paduma: lotus. So picture it: a trash heap on the side of a road, broken pots, peelings, dust. And growing out of it, a lotus, clean and fragrant. The verse goes on: so a disciple of the Buddha shines out by wisdom among people walking in darkness. In the verse, the flower doesn't wait for a clean pond. It comes up out of the refuse, and it's still fragrant. Buddhist tradition takes the lotus as a picture of exactly this: rooted in the mud, rising out of it, unstained. So the flower chapter ends not in a garden, but beside the road, on the heap, where a lot of real life happens.
screen: `A SCENT AGAINST THE WIND.` · `MANY GARLANDS FROM ONE HEAP.` · `MÜLLER'S LILY IS A LOTUS.` · `ROOTED IN THE MESS, UNSTAINED.` · then, large: `THE LOTUS ON THE HEAP.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Bring to mind one rough place in your life. A tired street you walk down. A difficult job. A home that's messier than you'd like. A hard stretch of this year. Now look there, gently, for one lotus. Something clean or kind or beautiful that grew right out of it. A neighbor who waves. A coworker who covers for you. A small courage you didn't know you had. Hold it in mind and breathe with it, not denying the heap, just seeing the flower too. The bell holds the time.
The lotus on the rubbish heap. Goodness growing clean and fragrant out of a rough place, its scent going even against the wind.

171.title: Long is the night (60–63)
171.hook: long is the night to the sleepless; the fool who knows he is a fool is wise so far
171.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote verse sixty-three to encourage humility in study, and the story of the two pickpockets is a popular teaching tale.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lotus on the rubbish heap, and your line: the lotus on the heap. What beauty did you find in a rough place? Day one hundred seventy-one, and chapter five: the fool.
screen: `THE LOTUS ON THE HEAP.`

segments.voice: Three in the morning, wide awake, and the clock seems broken. Every time you check, it's been four minutes. Or the last mile of a long hike, when your feet hurt and the trail keeps going, and that mile feels longer than the first five. Time stretches when things hurt. The fifth chapter of the Dhammapada begins with exactly those two pictures, and then adds a third that's much less comfortable. Today, verses sixty to sixty-three: long is the night.
screen: `3AM, AND THE CLOCK IS BROKEN.` → `THE LAST MILE OF THE HIKE.` → `A THIRD, LESS COMFORTABLE.`

segments.voice: Verse sixty, in Müller's English: “Long is the night to him who is awake; long is a mile to him who is tired; long is life to the foolish who do not know the true law.” Two ordinary pictures, and then the turn. Life itself drags on, round after round, for someone who never sees how things really are. Chapter five is called the fool, bala in Pali. The word also means a child, someone not grown up yet. It isn't about low intelligence. It's about not seeing. Verse sixty-one says it's better to travel alone than with a fool. Verse sixty-two describes one: my sons, my wealth, he thinks, and it torments him, though he doesn't even own himself, let alone his sons or his money. Then comes verse sixty-three, and it's a gift: “The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.” The commentary tells it with two pickpockets who went to hear the Buddha teach, planning to work the crowd. One of them started listening, and forgot to steal. The teaching went in, and the story says he saw the truth right there. The other stole a coin and went home. His wife, that evening, mocked the first thief for coming home with nothing, calling him wise. And the Buddha, hearing of it, spoke the verse. The one who knew he didn't know was the one who could learn. There's real relief in that. You don't have to be wise to begin. You only have to notice where you aren't.
screen: `THE NIGHT, THE MILE, THE LIFE.` · `BALA — THE ONE WHO DOESN'T SEE.` · `MY SONS, MY WEALTH.` · `TWO PICKPOCKETS AT A SERMON.` · then, large: `WISE SO FAR.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Now, with no shame at all, bring to mind one thing you don't really know, but sometimes act as if you do. A topic you nod along to. A skill you bluff. Something about the people you love that you've assumed and never asked. Just see it. Let yourself be the first pickpocket, the one who forgot to steal because he started listening. See whether admitting it brings any ease, a small weight put down. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Long is the night. Time stretches for the sleepless, the tired and the one who doesn't see; the fool who knows it is already wise so far.
screen: `LONG IS THE NIGHT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: wise so far. Today, say out loud, to someone, one thing you don't know. “I don't know” counts. Day one hundred seventy-one.

172.title: The spoon and the soup (64–68)
172.hook: a fool beside a wise person all his life knows the truth no more than a spoon tastes the soup
172.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the spoon-and-soup verses to stress that being near teachers or temples is not the same as taking the teaching in, and to encourage wholehearted listening.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, long is the night, and your line: wise so far. Did you say “I don't know” to someone? Day one hundred seventy-two.
screen: `LONG IS THE NIGHT — WISE SO FAR.`

segments.voice: A ladle sits in a pot of soup at a family dinner. It has been in there for hours. It has stirred the onions, the broth, the spices. It's touched every drop. It has been closer to that soup than anyone at the table. And it has tasted absolutely nothing. Meanwhile, a guest walks in, takes one spoonful off the ladle, and knows the whole soup in a second. The Dhammapada puts those two side by side, and asks what makes the difference. Today, verses sixty-four to sixty-eight: the spoon and the soup.
screen: `A LADLE IN THE POT FOR HOURS.` → `IT HAS TASTED NOTHING.` → `ONE SIP, AND THE GUEST KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Verse sixty-four, in Müller's English: “If a fool be associated with a wise man even all his life, he will perceive the truth as little as a spoon perceives the taste of soup.” And its twin, verse sixty-five: “If an intelligent man be associated for one minute only with a wise man, he will soon perceive the truth, as the tongue perceives the taste of soup.” A lifetime next to wisdom, or one minute. What makes the difference isn't how close you are. It's whether you taste. The commentary tells verse sixty-four about an elder named Udayi who liked to sit in the teacher's seat. Visiting monks assumed he must be learned and asked him questions, and he couldn't answer a single one. He'd been near the teaching for years, like the ladle. Verse sixty-five goes with a lively story from the monastic rulebook: thirty young men out for a day in the woods with their wives, one of them with a hired companion, who ran off with their things. Chasing her, they met the Buddha sitting under a tree and asked if he'd seen a woman go by. He asked them: which is better, to go looking for a woman, or to go looking for yourselves? They sat down to listen. In one conversation, the story says, they understood, and asked to become monks. Verses sixty-six to sixty-eight add a practical test. A deed is well done when you don't regret it afterward, when you remember it with gladness. So this isn't about being near good things. It's about letting them in.
screen: `A LIFETIME, LIKE A SPOON.` · `ONE MINUTE, LIKE A TONGUE.` · `UDAYI IN THE TEACHER'S SEAT.` · `LOOKING FOR YOURSELVES.` · then, large: `TASTE THE SOUP.`

segments.voice: Let's taste something now. Sit and take one breath, and taste it: the cool at the nostrils, the rise of the chest, the small pause at the top, the long release. Not thinking about breathing. Tasting it. Then another. All day the breath has gone on unnoticed, like a ladle stirring the pot. Now, for a couple of minutes, be the tongue. And later today, bring the same thing to one conversation: really taste what the other person is saying. The bell holds the time.
The spoon and the soup. A spoon in the soup all its life tastes nothing; a tongue tastes it in a moment.
screen: `THE SPOON AND THE SOUP — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: taste the soup. Today, in one conversation, stop half-listening and taste it fully, as if you'd only get one sip. Day one hundred seventy-two.

173.title: Milk that turns slowly (69–75)
173.hook: an evil deed, like fresh milk, does not turn at once; it smolders like fire under ash
173.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the milk and ash verses to explain kamma: actions have results, but those results may ripen slowly, which is why small harmful acts are taken seriously.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the spoon and the soup, and your line: taste the soup. Which conversation did you really taste? Day one hundred seventy-three, the end of the fool chapter.
screen: `THE SPOON AND THE SOUP — TASTE THE SOUP.`

segments.voice: In the days before refrigerators, milk came straight from the cow into a pail. If you left it on the counter, nothing happened right away. It looked fine. It smelled fine at lunch. By evening, maybe still fine. And then, the next morning, it had turned: sour, thick, undrinkable. The change was happening the whole time. You just couldn't see it yet. Most of us have lived through a version of that: a small lie, a shortcut, a harsh word, that seemed to cost nothing, until one day it did. Today, verses sixty-nine to seventy-five: milk that turns slowly.
screen: `MILK IN A PAIL ON THE COUNTER.` → `FINE AT LUNCH. FINE BY EVENING.` → `THEN IT HAS TURNED.`

segments.voice: Verse sixty-nine, in Müller's English: “As long as the evil deed done does not bear fruit, the fool thinks it is like honey; but when it ripens, then the fool suffers grief.” Like honey. The shortcut feels sweet, because nothing has happened yet. Then verse seventy-one: “An evil deed, like newly-drawn milk, does not turn (suddenly); smouldering, like fire covered by ashes, it follows the fool.” Two pictures. Fresh milk that sours slowly. And a fire banked under ash: the surface gray and cool-looking, the coals underneath still hot, waiting for a careless foot. This is the Buddhist teaching of kamma in its most down-to-earth form. Actions have results, but the results often ripen slowly, and that delay is exactly what fools us. The delay isn't proof that nothing happened. It's just the milk, still on the counter. The rest of the chapter warns about something just as quiet: knowledge used for the wrong ends, and wanting a reputation, the best seat, authority over others. Then the chapter ends with a verse many people carry for life, verse seventy-five: “One is the road that leads to wealth, another the road that leads to Nirvana.” Not a condemnation of earning a living. A reminder that the two roads point in different directions, and a person should know which one they're walking. So chapter five, the fool, closes. Long is the night. Wise so far. Taste the soup. And now: it turns slowly. Which is also good news. Good deeds ripen slowly too.
screen: `SWEET AS HONEY, UNTIL IT RIPENS.` · `MILK THAT DOESN'T TURN AT ONCE.` · `FIRE UNDER THE ASH.` · `TWO ROADS: WEALTH AND NIBBANA.` · then, large: `IT TURNS SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Let one slow consequence come to mind, from your own life. Maybe something you did long ago that only caught up with you later. Or a good habit that took months to show its fruit: a friendship tended, a skill practiced, a kindness that came back. Just notice the delay. The gap between the deed and the result. Then look at today, gently. Is anything sitting on the counter right now, that you might want to deal with before it turns? Breathe with that, without judgment. The bell holds the time.
Milk that turns slowly. An action's results often ripen late, like fresh milk souring or fire hidden under ash.

174.title: Hidden treasure (76–81)
174.hook: follow the one who points out your faults as if showing buried treasure; a solid rock is not shaken by wind
174.howItsDone: In Buddhist monastic life, being 'easy to admonish' is counted a virtue, and monks formally invite correction from one another, as at the end of the rains retreat.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, milk that turns slowly, and your line: it turns slowly. What slow consequence did you trace back? Day one hundred seventy-four, and chapter six: the wise.
screen: `MILK THAT TURNS SLOWLY — IT TURNS SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: A boss says the report missed the point. A friend says you've been short lately. A kid says, “you're on your phone again.” Being corrected stings, and the quick response is easy to predict: heat in the face, a defense ready on the tongue, maybe a small list of the other person's faults, just in case. The sixth chapter of the Dhammapada starts somewhere else. It treats the person who corrects you like someone handing over a map to buried gold. Today, verses seventy-six to eighty-one: hidden treasure.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU DIDN'T WANT TO HEAR.` → `HEAT IN THE FACE.` → `A MAP TO BURIED GOLD.`

segments.voice: Chapter six is called pandita, the wise one. Verse seventy-six says: if you find a wise person who shows you what to avoid and corrects you, follow them as you'd follow someone who shows you where treasure is hidden. It will go better for you, not worse. The commentary tells it about an old man named Radha, so poor that the monks weren't sure he should be ordained. Sariputta, one of the Buddha's chief disciples, remembered that Radha had once given him a single spoonful of food, and took him on. The story says Radha took every correction gladly, never resenting it, and he thrived. Verse seventy-seven adds that the wise should admonish and hold others back from harm; the good will love them for it, only the bad won't. Then verse eighty, a lovely picture of craftsmen: “Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.” And verse eighty-one: “As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.” Put the two together. Correction is treasure. And blame and praise are both just wind. The wise person doesn't need praise to feel steady, and doesn't collapse under blame. They listen for what's useful, like Radha, and let the rest blow past. That's why the rock doesn't shake. Not because nothing hits it. Because it's rooted deeper than the weather.
screen: `PANDITA — THE WISE ONE.` · `CORRECTION AS BURIED TREASURE.` · `RADHA TAKES CORRECTION GLADLY.` · `BLAME AND PRAISE ARE BOTH WIND.` · then, large: `THE ROCK DOESN'T SHAKE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone who once corrected you, and was right. A teacher, a parent, a coach, a friend who said the hard thing. Remember the sting of it. Then remember what it gave you, what you learned or changed because of it. Let a little gratitude come, if it wants to. Then feel yourself as a rock: heavy, grounded, breathing. Let a word of praise drift by in your mind, and a word of blame. Both are wind. The rock doesn't shake. The bell holds the time.
Pandita. The wise one, who treats correction like treasure, fashions themselves like a craftsman, and stands like a rock in blame and praise.
screen: `PANDITA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the rock doesn't shake. Today, thank someone who corrected you, a message or a word. Tell them what it gave you. Day one hundred seventy-four.

175.title: The deep lake (82–89)
175.hook: the wise grow calm like a deep, clear, still lake; few reach the other shore
175.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the image of a still, clear lake for a settled mind in meditation, and the other shore appears as an image for nibbana in chants and teachings.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, pandita, the wise one, and your line: the rock doesn't shake. Did you thank someone who corrected you? Day one hundred seventy-five, the end of the week, and the end of chapter six.
screen: `PANDITA — THE ROCK DOESN'T SHAKE.`

segments.voice: Stand at the edge of a shallow puddle and toss in a pebble. Mud clouds up everywhere, the whole thing churns, and it takes a long time to clear. Now picture a deep mountain lake early on a windless morning. You can see down through the water to stones far below, and the surface holds the whole sky: clouds, trees, the far ridge. Drop a pebble in, and the rings spread, and soften, and the lake is still again. Same pebble. Very different water. Today, verses eighty-two to eighty-nine: the deep lake.
screen: `A PEBBLE IN A PUDDLE.` → `A DEEP LAKE AT DAWN.` → `SAME PEBBLE, DIFFERENT WATER.`

segments.voice: Verse eighty-two, in Müller's English: “Wise people, after they have listened to the laws, become serene, like a deep, smooth, and still lake.” Deep, smooth, still. Three qualities. Deep: things reach far down without stirring up mud. Smooth: the surface isn't whipped around by every gust. Still: it reflects what's there, instead of distorting it. Verse eighty-three says good people walk on, whatever happens: they aren't lifted up by pleasure or thrown down by pain. It's yesterday's rock, turned to water. Then verses eighty-five and eighty-six bring in a picture that will come back on this path: the other shore. “Few are there among men who arrive at the other shore (become Arhats); the other people here run up and down the shore.” Picture a riverbank crowded with people, all busy, running this way and that along the edge. Very few actually cross. The other shore is freedom, nibbana; this side is the round of wanting and worrying. Verse eighty-six says those who live by the teaching will cross over. And the chapter closes by describing the wise as leaving the dark and following the bright, and shining in this world. Look back over the week. The bee. The lotus on the heap. Long is the night. The spoon and the soup. Milk that turns slowly. The rock that doesn't shake. And now still water. And the week ends on the simplest of its pictures: water, left alone long enough to settle.
screen: `DEEP, SMOOTH AND STILL.` · `NOT LIFTED, NOT THROWN DOWN.` · `RUNNING UP AND DOWN THE SHORE.` · `THE WEEK, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `STILL WATER.`

segments.voice: Sit like still water. Let the body settle first, heavy and at rest, like a lake in its bed. Then let the breath slow down on its own. Thoughts will drop in like pebbles. When one does, don't grab it and don't chase the ripples. Just watch the rings spread, and soften, and fade. Notice that the lake doesn't have to do anything for the water to go still again. It only has to stop stirring. The bell holds the time.
The deep lake. The wise grow serene like deep, smooth, still water, and few cross to the other shore.
screen: `THE DEEP LAKE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: still water. Today, when something stirs you up, stop stirring for three breaths, and let it settle before you answer. Day one hundred seventy-five.

screen: `DAY 175 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BIRDS IN THE SKY.`

fork.setup: a thought drops into your sitting like a pebble into a lake. what does still water do?
options: chase the ripples to stop them.
let the rings spread and fade on their own.
throw in a bigger stone to cover it.
fork.reveal: the lake doesn't have to do anything to go still again. it only has to stop stirring.

original.note: Pali: a lake, from verse eighty-two: 'yathapi rahado gambhiro,' like a deep lake.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm person is someone nothing reaches.
what it means: things reach the wise deeply, but don't churn up mud; the surface settles and reflects clearly.
what a scholar hears: 'rahado gambhiro vippasanno anavilo': deep, very clear, unstirred; 'paragu,' one gone to the far shore, is a standing epithet of the awakened.
